content: Lead (Pb) possesses four stable isotopes: 204Pb, 206Pb, 207Pb, and 208Pb. Additionally, it has one commonly encountered radiogenic isotope, 202Pb, which has a half-life of approximately 53,000 years. The standard atomic mass of lead is 207.2(1) atomic mass units (u). Lead is the heaviest element known to have a stable isotope.9 × 10^19 years. Several isotopes of lead are formed as part of the radioactive decay chains of actinium, radium, and thorium. These isotopes are historically referred to by specific names: 206Pb is known as radium G. 207Pb is referred to as actinium D. 208Pb is called thorium D. 210Pb is known as radium D, radio-lead, or radiolead. 211Pb is referred to as actinium B. 212Pb is called thorium B. 214Pb is known as radium B. The isotope 206Pb represents the final stable product of the uranium/radium decay series, originating from uranium-238 (U-238). Similarly, 207Pb is the terminal isotope of the actinium decay series, which begins with uranium-235 (U-235). Lastly, 208Pb is the end product of the thorium decay series, which starts with thorium-232 (Th-232). The evaluated isotopic composition of lead applies to most, but not all, commercially available samples. Variations in isotope abundances and atomic mass are influenced by natural processes, and the reported ranges are generally applicable to typical terrestrial materials. However, geologically exceptional samples exist in which the isotopic composition falls outside the standard range. For such specimens, the uncertainty in the atomic mass may exceed the stated values. It is important to note that values marked with a are not derived solely from experimental data but are partially based on systematic trends. Spins with weakly supported assignments are enclosed in parentheses. Uncertainties are expressed in a concise format within parentheses following the last significant digits. These uncertainty values represent one standard deviation, except for isotopic composition and standard atomic mass values provided by IUPAC, which use expanded uncertainties.
